6758.t: Of Anatolian origin, possibly related to the Hittite 𒈪𒂖𒆷𒉿𒀭𒁕 (Millawanda). Compare Mycenaean Greek 𐀖𐀨𐀴𐀍 (mi-ra-ti-jo, “Miletian”), 𐀖𐀨𐀴𐀊 (mi-ra-ti-ja, “women from Miletus”).

6774.t: From πόντος (póntos, “sea”), attested in Mycenaean Greek as 𐀡𐀵 (po-to).

6796.t: Anatolian name, from Hittite 𒌷𒋻𒊭 (Tarša), possibly from 𒋫𒅈𒆪 (Tarku), a god. The name may have entered Greek through Akkadian 𒆳𒋻𒋛𒋛 (Tarsisi).

6720.t: Pre-Greek, likely Anatolian. Compare with Hittite 𒌷𒄭𒇷𒅅𒋡 (ᵁᴿᵁḫi-li-ik-ka₄ /⁠Ḫilika⁠/), and Luwian 𔗒𔔹𔗧𔔂 (hi-li-ka^(URBS) /⁠Ḫilikka⁠/) and 𔗒𔖱𔓯𔗧𔔂 (hi+ra/i-i-ka^(URBS) /⁠Ḫirikka⁠/).

6791.t: Uncertain, but possibly from σπάρτον (spárton, “rope, cable”), a reference to the cords laid as the city's foundation boundaries, though this could be folk etymology.

6743.t: Likely of Anatolian origin, but of uncertain meaning: compare Hittite 𒇻𒊌𒅗𒊑 (“to light up”), and the placename Λυκαονία (Lukaonía) (related to Lukka).

6766.t: From πατήρ (pătḗr, “father”) + -κλῆς (-klês, “fame”) + -ος (-os). Compare Κλεόπατρος (Kleópatros, “Cleopater”), which contains the same components in the opposite order.

6770.t: Perhaps Pre-Greek, perhaps from πέρθω (pérthō). More at Perseus.

6777.t: The name may be from Anatolian, but it is also formally equivalent to σίδη (sídē, “pomegranate”). Both the city and fruit could be from this Anatolian language and of the same meaning.

6705.t: From δόσις (dósis, “gift”) + θεός (theós, “god”). For the semantics, compare Θεόδωρος (Theódōros).

6798.t: From τρι- (tri-, “three”) + πόλις (pólis, “city”); however, for Tripolis in Phoenicia, the name was possibly formed by folk etymology from an earlier, phonetically similar, Semitic name.

6790.t: Borrowed from Biblical Hebrew שִּׁילוֹחַ (Shiloaḥ), whose meaning "gushing forth" is also rendered in Greek as ἀπεσταλμένος (apestalménos, “having been sent”), passive perfect participle of ἀποστέλλω (apostéllō)

6767.t: Uncertain; cognate with Mycenaean Greek 𐀞𐀊𐀺𐀚 (pa-ja-wo-ne).
